children: UPI payments for capital-market transactions will attract a 0.02 percent Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) from October 15, but analysts expect little impact on retail investors, with the cost to be absorbed by brokers and asset management companies. The bigger impact, they say, could be on broker margins, particularly for discount brokers handling frequent pay-ins from active and intraday traders.

MDR is essentially a fee charged within the payments ecosystem for processing a merchant transaction. In the case of capital-market payments, the 0.02 percent charge will be borne by regulated entities such as brokers and asset management companies, rather than being directly passed on to retail investors.

For context, at 0.02 percent, the MDR on a Rs 1 lakh transaction would work out to Rs 20, while the Rs 300 cap limits the cost on larger transactions. The capital-market rate is also significantly lower than the 0.4 percent MDR applicable to other person-to-merchant UPI transactions above Rs 2,000.

Market expert Sunil Subramaniam expects the impact on retail investors to be minimal, particularly for those investing for the long term. With SIPs carrying zero MDR and the cost of larger lump-sum transactions being absorbed by AMCs or other regulated entities, he does not expect a meaningful change in investor behaviour.

The bigger impact, according to Subramaniam, could emerge among active and intraday traders. He expects trading volumes themselves to remain largely unaffected, but brokers could face some margin pressure because of frequent, same-day UPI pay-ins. This could be more relevant for discount brokers, which operate on relatively thin margins and may look to change the payment behaviour of frequent users.

Subramaniam expects brokers to promote alternatives such as direct net banking, NEFT/RTGS virtual accounts and secondary-market UPI block mechanisms, which can reduce the need for repeated ad-hoc UPI pay-ins.

Sunny Agrawal, head of fundamental equity research at SBI Securities, said the impact will depend on the financial instrument involved as well as the existing fee structure for that particular instrument.

This means the effect may not be uniform across stocks, mutual funds and other capital-market transactions. For investors, however, the relatively low MDR and the restrictions on passing the cost directly to customers should limit the immediate impact.

NSE Managing Director and CEO Ashishkumar Chauhan also expects some near-term impact on trading activity routed through UPI. He said MDR "might impact trading volumes via UPI in the short term, but is likely to stabilise in the long term."

title: UPI MDR on stocks, MFs: Investors largely insulated, but brokers may feel the pinch
